curriculum.lesson_evidence: Improvisation means making up a scene together by accepting an offer and staying inside the fiction. An offer is any new fact a partner gives you, such as a place, a problem, or a feeling. Accepting means you treat that fact as true in the story, even if you did not plan it. The fiction is the pretend world you both agree to keep alive, so you answer as the character rather than stepping out to say you do not know the plot. There is no published play to memorise in this lesson. The original fiction is a school library where Sam has lost a borrowed book called the blue nature guide. When the librarian says the guide was due yesterday, Sam's job is to accept that fact and add one small detail that could really happen in the library. Writing the lines is the work. Acting them out is optional, and only with an adult nearby.

lesson.guided_practice:
PRACTISE BEFORE READING THE FEEDBACK
In the lost-book fiction your partner says, 'I saw the blue nature guide on the art-room windowsill after lunch.' Which next line accepts that offer and keeps Sam inside the library story?

FEEDBACK
Sam should ask the art teacher whether the guide is still beside the clay sink. That line treats the windowsill as a true fact and keeps both players inside the library story. It also gives a next action, so the partner can offer something new. Saying 'I never had a library book' would cancel the offer, and saying 'I do not know the plot' would step out of the fiction.

WATCH FOR
Blocking the offer by denying the lost book, or stepping out to say the plot is unknown, stops the scene. A block such as 'No, I never borrowed a guide' leaves your partner with nothing true to build on. Accepting does not mean Sam caused the problem. It means Sam agrees the problem exists inside the story, then helps the story continue.
lesson.independent_task:
INDEPENDENT EVIDENCE
Write two in-role lines that accept a new offer about a missing sports-shed key and an unlocked shed door. Partner: 'The shed key is gone and the door is standing open.' Line one accepts that fact as the student on duty. Line two adds one new detail that keeps the fiction going. Then name the offer you accepted in one sentence. Use this shed scene, not the library book. Writing is the evidence. Performing is optional and needs an adult nearby.

Write a short reflection naming one artistic choice you changed and why. Movement or instrument work is optional, adult-supervised and can be described instead.
